use.e: From Middle English use, from Old French us, from Latin ūsus (“use, custom, skill, habit”), from past participle stem of ūtor (“use”). Middle English nutte (“use”) from Old English nytt; as well as Old English fricu and Old English sidu.
From Middle English usen, from Old French user (“use, employ, practice”), from Medieval Latin usare (“use”), frequentative form of past participle stem of Latin uti (“to use”).

used.e: From Middle English used, equivalent to use + -ed.
used.g: That is or has or have been used.

useful.g: Having a practical or beneficial use.

usher.e: From Middle English ussher, uscher, usscher, from Anglo-Norman usser and Old French ussier, uissier (“porter, doorman”) (compare French huissier), from Vulgar Latin *ustiārius (“doorkeeper”), from Latin ōstiārius, from ōstium (“door”). Probably a doublet of ostiary and huissier.
usher.g: A person, in a church, cinema etc., who escorts people to their seats.

usual.e: From Middle English usual, from Old French usuel, from Latin ūsuālis (“for use, fit for use, also of common use, customary, common, ordinary, usual”), from ūsus (“use, habit, custom”), from the past participle stem of ūtī (“to use”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃eyt- (“to take along, fetch”).

usurer.e: Anglo-Norman, from Old French usurier, Latin ūsūra (“interest”).
usurer.g: A person who loans money to others and charges interest, particularly at an exorbitant, exploitative, or illegal rate.

usurp.e: From Middle English usurpen, from Old French usurper, from Latin ūsūrpō.
usurp.g: To seize and hold or use (powers, an office, a coat of arms, a right or copyright, etc) from another, without right (usually by illegitimate

usurper.e: From Middle English usurper, usurpour, usurpur, from Middle French usurpeur; equivalent to usurp + -er.

usury.e: From Middle English usurie, from Latin ūsūria, from ūsūra (“lending at interest, usury”) from ūsus (“use”), from stem of ūtī (“to use”).
usury.g: An exorbitant rate of interest, in excess of any legal rates or at least immorally.
